passage:
Himani: hey, can I ask how you ended up in urban planning? You never said
Shalini: long story lol
Himani: I've got time. Did you always want it?
Shalini: no, I studied accounts. Then I spent a year helping my aunt's cooperative map water pipes and got hooked
Himani: what was the first thing that hooked you?
Shalini: standing in a lane with an old man who showed me where the water used to flow before the road was built
Himani: that sounds like a real moment
Shalini: it was. most people ask about the salary 😅
Himani: I'm more curious what you'd tell the younger you
Shalini: to not be embarrassed about the detour. thanks for asking 🙂

qa.q: What did Shalini study before urban planning?
qa.a: Shalini studied accounts.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling while asking these questions?
qa.a: Himani was curious and warm, wanting to know about Shalini's path without judging it.

qa.q: What kind of follow-up question worked best in this chat?
qa.a: Open questions about a moment, like what first hooked Shalini, invited a story. Himani listened and did not offer advice or compare.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt about being asked instead of being asked about the salary?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt seen and pleased, since most people ask about the salary and this question invited a real story about the detour. 🙂

grounding: A young adult asks a colleague open questions about their path and listens without judging, which builds a bond.

passage:
Anand sat on the stool in Salma's tailoring shop in the bazaar while she pinned a hem. Instead of talking about himself he asked, "How did you start this shop?"
Salma laughed. "Nobody asks that." She had begun with one borrowed machine in her father's storeroom, she said, sewing school uniforms at night after her shifts at the ginning mill.
"Weren't you scared?"
"Terrified. My brothers said a woman can't run a shop." She bit off a thread.
"And what did you do?"
"Ran it."
Anand didn't say "you should have" or offer advice. He nodded and asked how she'd taught her first apprentice. Salma pulled up a second stool. "Sit properly. This will take a while."

qa.q: What did Salma start with, according to her story?
qa.a: Salma began with one borrowed machine in her father's storeroom.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling as he listened to Salma?
qa.a: Anand was curious and respectful, wanting to hear her story without adding judgement.

qa.q: What could Anand ask next to keep the conversation going without giving advice?
qa.a: Anand could ask what the hardest week was, or what Salma is proudest of, and keep listening as he did about the apprentice.

qa.q: What is it like for Salma when someone asks how she started the shop?
qa.a: Salma is probably pleased and a little surprised, since she laughed that nobody asks. Being asked let her tell the story of her fear and her stubbornness. 🙂

grounding: A young adult asks an elder open questions about her path and listens without judging.

passage: Tuan had worked beside Emeka at the Manchester water-treatment office for four months and knew only that Emeka took his tea black and left at five sharp. The team joked that Emeka was "the quiet one who doesn't want to be here." On a slow Friday, Tuan pulled his chair over. "Can I ask how you got into this work?" Emeka looked surprised. Then he told him: he had taught chemistry in Lagos for eleven years, moved for his daughter's medical treatment, and retrained at forty. He left at five because he collected her from the hospital. Tuan didn't interrupt, except to ask, "What did you miss most about teaching?" Emeka smiled for the first time Tuan could remember. "The moment a student understands." The next Monday, Tuan asked Emeka to explain the new filtration report to the interns.

qa.q: How many years had Emeka taught chemistry in Lagos?
qa.a: Eleven years.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when Tuan asked about his path?
qa.a: He seemed surprised, then warmed and pleased, smiling for the first time Tuan could remember as he talked about teaching.

qa.q: Which part of Tuan's approach made the conversation work?
qa.a: He asked open questions and listened without interrupting or judging, which let Emeka share far more than the team had assumed.

qa.q: How might the team's view of Emeka change if they heard this?
qa.a: They might stop seeing him as 'the quiet one who doesn't want to be here' and understand why he leaves at five.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking a colleague open questions about his path and listening without judging, which builds a bond and breaks a stereotype.

passage: At 3 am in the hospital canteen, Raghav, a first-year resident, sat down opposite Nilesh, the ward attendant who always had the trolley ready before anyone asked. For six months they had only exchanged "thank you" and "welcome." Raghav was too tired to scroll his phone. "Nilesh bhai, how long have you worked here?" "Nine years." "What made you choose it?" Nilesh laughed. "Choose? My father was ill here. I stayed." Raghav leaned in. "And now?" Nilesh hesitated, then took a thick book out of his bag. Law. "Final year, evening college." Raghav didn't say "Wow, really?" in the surprised voice Nilesh probably expected. He asked, "Which subject do you like best?" "Constitutional law." They talked until the pager went off. After that, Raghav greeted him by name every shift, and asked how the exams were going.

qa.q: How long had Nilesh worked at the hospital?
qa.a: Nine years.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's hesitation before showing the book suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt a little unsure or guarded, perhaps worried about being judged or doubted.

qa.q: What did Raghav avoid that helped Nilesh open up?
qa.a: He avoided a surprised 'Wow, really?' and simply asked which subject Nilesh liked best, treating his studies as normal and interesting.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Raghav greets him by name every shift?
qa.a: He would probably feel seen and respected, more than just the person with the trolley.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking a colleague open questions about his path and listening without judgement, building a bond.

passage:
Dear Santosh uncle,

I'm leaving the building next week, and I wanted to thank you properly.

When I moved in, I thought you were just the watchman who opened the gate. One night the lift broke and we sat on the steps, and I asked where you grew up. You told me about the orange orchards in Nagpur, and your wife's pickles, and the two years you drove a truck across the Deccan.

After that I kept asking, and you kept answering. You never asked me why a girl from Kerala was living alone in Pune, and I tried never to assume anything about you either.

You taught me more about this city than anyone. I'll miss our evening chai at the gate.

With love,
Elizabeth

qa.q: Where did Santosh uncle grow up?
qa.a: Near the orange orchards in Nagpur.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel about leaving the building?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels grateful and a little sad, missing their evening chai at the gate.

qa.q: What small habit built the friendship between Elizabeth and Santosh uncle?
qa.a: Asking open questions about his life and listening without assuming, starting with a chat on the steps when the lift broke.

qa.q: How might Santosh uncle have felt when Elizabeth kept asking about his life?
qa.a: He probably felt valued and respected, seen as a person with a story rather than just the man at the gate.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking an older man open questions about his life and listening without judging, which built a warm bond.

passage: So I have to tell you about Sabina Aunty from our office canteen. I'm Anjali, and for a whole year all I'd ever said to her was "one masala dosa, please". Honestly, I assumed she'd been making dosas all her life. Last Tuesday the canteen was empty because of the all-hands, so I asked, "How did you end up running this place?" And then I just listened. She played state-level hockey till twenty-two. She did a correspondence course in accounts while raising two kids, and she keeps the canteen's books herself, not just the kitchen. I asked what she'd do differently. She said, "Nothing. Maybe learn to drive earlier." We talked for forty minutes. I'd had her in a box without even knowing it. Now at lunch she asks about my project, and I ask about her grandson's hockey.

qa.q: What sport did Sabina Aunty play till twenty-two?
qa.a: She played state-level hockey.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel after the forty-minute talk?
qa.a: Anjali felt surprised and a little embarrassed at having boxed Sabina Aunty in, and much warmer toward her 😊

qa.q: What made Anjali's question work?
qa.a: It was open, "How did you end up running this place?", and Anjali listened without judging, so Sabina Aunty could tell her whole path.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sabina Aunty to be asked about her life?
qa.a: She may have felt seen and valued beyond the dosa counter, which is why she now asks about Anjali's project too.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking an older colleague open questions about her path and listening, which breaks an unnoticed stereotype.
